comments.text:
Houston has the right idea of in-filling rather than sprawling. You need clean, safe, affordable to moderately affordable housing that is either flexible (you can have an auxiliary unit or on-site business) or dense (minimal yard with frequent, well-maintained parks within a safe walking path. Keeping urban areas dense rather than suburban sprawl also makes public transit easier and as stated, encourages more walking & bike riding. Now, building up isn’t always the best option, especially in tornado prone areas… but being able to move dwellings closer to the road means you can have a larger, single story dwelling in the same footprint as a two story set 25ft back. 

I’m actually really pleased that my area in PA has brought back row housing. People can actually own them and there are no HOAs, so they’re getting painted fun colors. It’s wonderful!

comments.text:
Suburban sprawl (car-dependent suburbia) is the most pernicious development pattern imaginable and Texas is doing it in a way that's even worse than the rest of the country.  Surprised Wendover ended the video where he did, as that's the beginning of the Texas story of which we've only read the first chapter.  The critical problem with suburban sprawl is that it creates huge infrastructure commitments that persist indefinitely into the future and a very low tax base, thanks to low density, to pay for it.  

Strong Towns and Urban 3 have built their foundational message around this idea.  Low density and low amenities works.  High density and high density works.  But low density with high amenities is a recipe for financial disaster.

comments.text: I'd suspect there's some benefit to a consistant cultural ideal that hasn't yet hit its geographical limit.
